messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika is a 55-year-old Pacific Islander man who now works as a nanny for two school-aged children in an affluent Seattle neighborhood. He came to treatment months after the death of his adult daughter, who had been assaulted and left with catastrophic injuries before dying in the hospital. He can begin the story only in fragments. He remembers being called, driving in a panic, and then the hospital room: the stillness of her body, the visible injuries that his mind keeps returning to, and the sound in the room—machines, hurried voices, and his own daughter’s strained breathing before it stopped. When he tries to describe the sequence to other people, he loses the thread and stalls out, as if the memory breaks apart in his hands. What comes back most sharply are flashes and sounds, and with them a crushing wave of grief that feels as fresh as the day she died.

In the weeks after the funeral, Mika had come to believe that the death revealed something final about him. He was certain he had failed in the most basic duty a father has, that he should have protected her and did not. The thought was not abstract; it settled into his sense of himself. He described feeling weak, the kind of man who could not keep his own child safe, and at times he spoke about himself as if he were barely a person in the aftermath, more like something numb and used up than fully human. These meanings attached themselves to the memory whenever it surfaced. Each attempt to recall the hospital brought not only images and the echo of what he had heard there, but also the verdict he passed on himself. He did not simply remember losing his daughter; he remembered it as proof of weakness and failure, and that made the memory harder to hold onto in a coherent way before he broke off, overwhelmed by grief.

Those same beliefs also shaped what he noticed and feared in ordinary life. Because he saw himself as the father who had not protected his child, reminders of injured bodies became almost unbearable. A glimpse of an exposed elbow, a badly bruised knee, or a child clutching an arm on the playground could pull his attention with shocking force toward the parts of the body he had seen damaged in the hospital. News stories or casual conversation about families losing loved ones felt immediately dangerous to him, not just sad. He listened for them, tensed at them, and reacted as if each one confirmed again that terrible losses happen when someone fails to keep another person safe. Even mentions of other victims seemed to fasten onto his daughter in his mind.

His work has made these reactions especially difficult to contain. As a nanny, he spends his days packing lunches, walking the children to school, kneeling to tie shoes, checking scraped skin after recess, and helping with baths after muddy afternoons. In that setting, body-focused reminders are everywhere. If one of the children points to a bruise or asks him to look at a cut, Mika can feel himself go cold. Sometimes the sight instantly summons the auditory memory of the hospital—voices, monitors, the sounds around his daughter’s bed—and once that begins he is flooded by grief so intense he has to turn away and compose himself in the bathroom. When this happens, he is left thinking again that a stronger man would be able to stay present, that even now he is failing someone who depends on him.

Over time the memories and his self-judgments have tightened around each other. A reminder at work or in conversation brings back the hospital in jagged sensory pieces, especially the sounds, and he is overcome by sorrow; afterward he reads his reaction as further evidence that he is weak and somehow less than fully human. Then the next reminder lands even harder because he is already braced for what it says about him. He has become wary of school pickup chatter with other caregivers because conversations about illness, accidents, or bereaved families can ruin the rest of his day. He keeps his answers short when asked about his daughter, not because he does not want to speak of her, but because he knows he will lose the thread and be left hearing the hospital again.

What finally brought Mika in was an incident when one of the children fell, split the skin on his chin, and began crying for him. Mika managed the first aid, but the sight of the injury and the child’s frightened voice immediately transported him back to his daughter’s final hours. He later sat in his car shaking, consumed by grief and by the conviction that he should not be caring for anyone if he could not master himself. He is seeking help now because he is afraid that his daughter’s death has permanently turned him into a weak, emptied-out man who will always fail the people he loves, and because some part of him still hopes he might find a way to remember her without being destroyed by the memory each time it comes.
